abstract: One-stage partial nitritation/anammox systems provide a cost-effective and efficient approach to nitrogen removal, but its wide application for sewage treatment remains a challenge. Four key ecological dynamics determine its success: i) the protection of anammox bacteria from oxygen exposure by nitrifiers, ii) the inhibition of nitrite-oxidizing bacteria through residual ammonia accumulation, iii) the competition for oxygen among nitrifiers, and iv) the competition for nitrite between nitrite-oxidizing bacteria and anammox bacteria. Using a comprehensive Individual-based Model, we simulate the ecological interactions among microbial communities under relevant operational and environmental conditions, emphasizing the role of nitrite-oxidizing bacteria diversity by differentiating Nitrobacter, Nitrospira and Nitrotoga genera. Our simulation experiments identify and quantify the fundamental constraints when optimizing one-stage partial nitritation/anammox systems, particularly the challenge of suppressing nitrite-oxidizing bacteria while maintaining a strong anammox activity. Notably, our results show that the previously observed stratification between ammonia- and nitrite-oxidizing communities, does not indicate optimal nitrogen process partitioning. These findings highlight the limitations of relying solely on operational design to control community structure, as this approach may fail to ensure stable and efficient nitrogen removal across diverse conditions in one-stage partial nitritation/anammox systems.
